docs.title: Philly Civic Cloud
docs.text:
CodeForPhilly runs two Kubernetes clusters on Linode, sandbox and live, and each is described completely by a git repo. Change the repo, and a pipeline changes the cluster; nothing is applied by hand, and nothing runs that isn’t in the repo. Shared pieces (TLS, routing, PostgreSQL, backups) are run once for everyone, so a project brings its container image and a few files, and gets a hostname, a certificate, a database and a backup without building any of it.

Sandbox Live Repo cfp-sandbox-cluster cfp-live-cluster Hostnames *.sandbox.k8s.phl.io *.live.k8s.phl.io, plus real domains Purpose land it here first production

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
I’m on a project team and want my app running here. Start with the Guides: how deploys work, where your project lives in the repo, and how to add and use a database. About twenty minutes, in order.

My app is already here and I need a database. Skip to Add a database and Connect your app. Four files, no shared infrastructure touched.

I need to change a value, bump a version, or rotate a secret. Your project in the repo shows which files are yours, and How deploys work shows how to preview the change before it lands.

I’m operating the cluster. Operations covers upgrades, the echo service for checking connectivity, and the shared components. The agent-facing notes in each repo’s .claude/CLAUDE.md hold the current state of the cluster and the hard-won lessons.

I want to understand the pieces. Development describes the architecture inherited from the upstream cluster template; Reference is the one-page directory map and gotcha list for these clusters.

Questions go to #civic-cloud on the Code for Philly Slack.

docs.title: Access via Metabase
docs.text:
Metabase is available at https://metabase.sandbox.k8s.phl.io/

To be invited, post a request including your email address to the #cfp-data-pipeline Slack channel

docs.title: Access via psql
docs.text:
The PostgreSQL database port is exposed publically via a NodePort service, which means that port number is open on all nodes in the cluster and automatically proxied to PostgreSQL’s port regardless of which node it is actually running on.

As of this writing, one such IP is 45.33.79.76 but this is subject to change when that node is eventually recycled, so the warehouse could be connected to for administration with a command like:

psql -h 45.33.79.76 -p 30432 -U admin -d warehouse

The password can be found in VaultWarden under the cfp-data-pipeline organization within the item admin @ postgresql database.

docs.title: Add a user
docs.text:
To add a new PostgreSQL user to the warehouse:

  1. Connect via the admin user

  2. Create a new user:

    CREATE USER myusername WITH ENCRYPTED PASSWORD 'generate_a_password';

  3. Assign readonly role:

    GRANT readonly TO myusername;

docs.title: Initial setup
docs.text:
1. Create warehouse database in PostgreSQL:

    CREATE DATABASE warehouse;

  2. Create readonly warehouse role:

    CREATE ROLE readonly;

-- Grant access to existing tables
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO readonly;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO readonly;

-- Grant access to future tables
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO readonly;

  3. Set up user for metabase:

    CREATE USER metabase WITH ENCRYPTED PASSWORD 'GENERATE_A_PASSWORD_AND_SAVE_IN_VAULT';
GRANT readonly TO metabase;

docs.title: Exposing services (Gateway API)
docs.text:
Public services are exposed through Envoy Gateway and the Kubernetes Gateway API. This replaces the older ingress-nginx path (see Legacy: ingress-nginx).

The design rests on one rule, and most of the sharp edges below are consequences of getting it wrong:

A cluster decides where a service is reachable. An application decides what it serves. Neither declares the other’s half.

The cluster owns The application owns Gateway — hostnames, TLS, certificate issuer, gatewayClassName HTTPRoute — paths, backend Services, ports GatewayClass, the shared data plane, the HTTP→HTTPS redirect its own container ports and routing

Hostnames, TLS, and issuers differ between clusters and are negotiated across every app sharing the ingress — they are cluster facts. Paths and ports change when the app changes and belong in the same commit as that change — they are app facts. An app cannot correctly author cluster facts: it doesn’t know the cluster’s issuer name, cert Secret names, or Gateway class, and guessing wrong fails in ways that are hard to see (see Failure modes).

docs.title: Exposing a service
docs.text:
1. The cluster provides a Gateway named after the app, in the app’s namespace, with one HTTPS listener per hostname:

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: my-app
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  gatewayClassName: eg
  listeners:
    - name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
      port: 443
      hostname: my-app.sandbox.k8s.phl.io
      tls:
        mode: Terminate
        certificateRefs:
          - name: my-app-gw-tls        # cert-manager creates this from the annotation
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces:
          from: Same

cert-manager sees the cluster-issuer annotation and issues the certificate into the certificateRefs Secret automatically. No Certificate resource is written by hand.

2. The application ships an HTTPRoute that attaches to that Gateway by name and declares no hostnames:

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: my-app          # the Gateway the cluster provides
  # no hostnames — inherited from the Gateway's listeners
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path: { type: PathPrefix, value: / }
      backendRefs:
        - name: my-app
          port: 80

A route with no hostnames inherits them from the listeners it attaches to. So the same route file works unchanged in every environment — the Gateway supplies the hostname — and the app repo contains zero cluster facts. This is the mechanism that makes the ownership split practical; it is a supported part of the Gateway API and behaves correctly on Envoy Gateway.

When an app team ships routes from their own repository, this is all they ship: an HTTPRoute, attached by convention to a Gateway named after the app.

docs.title: HTTP, HTTPS, and certificates
docs.text:
• HTTP→HTTPS is handled once, globally. A single redirect HTTPRoute on the shared HTTP listener 301s everything to HTTPS. Per-app HTTPRoutes attach only to their per-app HTTPS Gateway — they do not each carry a redirect.
  • ACME challenges bypass the redirect automatically. cert-manager creates a short-lived HTTPRoute per challenge with an Exact path match on /.well-known/acme-challenge/…, which outranks the catch-all redirect under Gateway API precedence.
  • One LoadBalancer for all Gateways. The EnvoyProxy resource sets mergeGateways: true, so every Gateway shares one Envoy data plane and one cloud LoadBalancer. Without it, each Gateway provisions its own LB and cost multiplies. Do not disable it.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
These are not hypothetical — each one cost real time on a production cluster.

Certificate issuance depends on in-cluster reachability

cert-manager runs an HTTP-01 self-check from inside the cluster before it asks the CA to validate. So a solver the cluster cannot reach from within will never issue a cert, even if it works perfectly from the public internet.

This is what makes ingress-nginx-with-PROXY-protocol unusable for issuance once the in-cluster PROXY-header shim (hairpin-proxy) is removed: in-cluster traffic bypasses the load balancer that would add the header, so the backend drops the connection and the self-check fails silently. The general rule: a component in the request path that needs a header only the load balancer supplies is unreachable from inside the cluster. Envoy Gateway does not use PROXY protocol, so it is reachable in-cluster and its self-checks pass. Never enable ClientTrafficPolicy.enableProxyProtocol to recover client IPs without accounting for this.

Don’t leave gateway certs pending across a renewal window

If you pre-create per-app Gateways (and their pending ACME challenges) but delay the DNS cutover, those challenges sit pending indefinitely. A pending challenge holds its hostname’s slot in cert-manager’s scheduler, which will not run two HTTP-01 challenges for the same hostname at once — so it can silently starve the legacy certificate’s renewal for that same hostname. If you must pause mid-migration, remove the cluster-issuer annotation from the pre-created Gateways so no challenges exist to hold the slots.

A Challenge can outlive its Order and deadlock renewals

A cert-manager Challenge is owned by both its Order and the ClusterIssuer. Kubernetes garbage-collects a dependent only when all owners are gone, so a Challenge survives its Order’s deletion as a half-orphan: still processing, no controller driving it, no GC path to remove it — and still holding its scheduler slot. Symptom: kubectl get challenges -A shows a challenge pending for days with a sibling for the same dnsName stuck with an empty status. Delete the stale one by name. The CertChallengeStuck alert (shipped with Grafana alerting) catches this.

ListenerSet is not usable yet

Envoy Gateway before v1.8 does not reconcile ListenerSet — it watches XListenerSet and logs XListenerSet CRD not found, skipping XListenerSet watch. A ListenerSet applies cleanly to the API server and is then silently ignored, leaving the hostname with no listener and nothing in any log to say why. Use per-app Gateway resources with mergeGateways: true until the cluster’s Envoy Gateway is on v1.8+.

docs.title: Legacy: ingress-nginx
docs.text: ingress-nginx remains in the manifests for compatibility with services that haven’t moved to the Gateway API yet, but it is being retired and new services should not use it. The old flow — an Ingress with kubernetes.io/ingress.class: nginx — still functions where it already exists. When migrating an existing Ingress, mirror its routing faithfully in the HTTPRoute: multi-path Ingresses (e.g. /api to a backend, / to a frontend) and redirect-only hosts must be reproduced as explicit HTTPRoute rules, or behavior changes silently at cutover.

docs.title: Ingress (legacy)
docs.text:
Public services are now exposed through the Gateway API — see Exposing services (Gateway API).

ingress-nginx and the Ingress resource remain in the manifests for compatibility with services that predate the migration, but they are being retired. New services should use the Gateway API. When moving an existing Ingress to an HTTPRoute, reproduce its routing exactly — see the migration note at the end of the Gateway page.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Configure and deploy a public ingress for sealed-secrets on the cluster
  • Install the kubeseal client command on your local workstation from the latest stable release: https://github.com/bitnami-labs/sealed-secrets/releases

docs.title: Configure public certificate
docs.text:
Place the public URL for the target cluster’s sealed secret’s certificate into the SEALED_SECRETS_CERT environment variable:

export SEALED_SECRETS_CERT=https://sealed-secrets.sandbox.k8s.phl.io/v1/cert.pem

docs.title: Encrypt secrets to cluster repository
docs.text:
Create a Kubernetes Secret manifest containing one or more key+value pair, and then use the kubeseal client to encrypt it into a SealedSecret manifest. The target namespace must be provided and will become part of the encryption such that the secret can only be loaded into that namespace. Commit the sealed secret to the cluster’s repository under the path ${project_namespace}.secrets/ where it will be added to the cluster’s deployed manifests:

kubeseal \
    --namespace "my-project" \
    -f my-secret.yaml \
    -w ~/Repositories/my-cluster/my-project.secrets/my-secret.yaml

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
The Getting Started section provides content covering:

  • Provisioning and initially deploying the cluster
  • Manual setup steps for included services
  • Onboarding new users into workflows

docs.title: Grafana SMTP & certificate alerting
docs.text:
The template ships certificate alert rules (in k8s-common/grafana/default-values.yaml) that email the cluster’s operators when a certificate stops renewing. Grafana sends that mail through Postmark, and the credential, sender, and recipient list come from a grafana-smtp Secret in the grafana namespace.

Until this Secret exists, Grafana still runs and the rules still evaluate — they just can’t deliver. Creating it turns delivery on.

docs.title: Why this is a Secret, and why Grafana rather than Alertmanager
docs.text:
Postmark’s server token is both the SMTP username and the password. Prometheus Alertmanager can read the SMTP password from a file but has no way to read the username from one, so on a public GitOps repo the token would end up committed in plaintext. Grafana reads both from a Secret as environment variables, exposing nothing — which is why alerting lives in Grafana here.

The recipient list lives in the Secret too: it’s usually personal addresses, and this keeps them out of a public repo.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
Key Value user Postmark server token password the same Postmark server token from-address a verified Postmark sender for this cluster (e.g. alerts@example.org) from-name the sender name shown in alert emails — name the cluster so its origin is obvious at a glance, e.g. CodeForPhilly — Live recipients semicolon-separated list, e.g. a@example.org;b@example.org

The from-address must be a verified sender signature (or under a verified domain) in the Postmark server, or Postmark rejects the mail. Set from-name distinctly per cluster — when several clusters share one Postmark server and email the same people, it’s the only thing in the inbox that says which cluster fired.

docs.title: Create it
docs.text:
Sealed into the cluster repo (recommended — survives a cluster rebuild):

TOKEN='<postmark-server-token>'
kubectl create secret generic grafana-smtp \
    --namespace grafana \
    --dry-run=client -o json \
    --from-literal=user="$TOKEN" \
    --from-literal=password="$TOKEN" \
    --from-literal=from-address='alerts@example.org' \
    --from-literal=from-name='CodeForPhilly — Live' \
    --from-literal=recipients='a@example.org;b@example.org' \
  | kubeseal --format yaml \
      --controller-namespace sealed-secrets --controller-name sealed-secrets \
  > grafana/grafana-smtp.sealed.yaml

Commit the sealed file. For a quick non-GitOps setup, drop the kubeseal pipe and apply the plain Secret directly instead — but never commit an unsealed one.

docs.title: Verify delivery
docs.text:
Don’t assume a rendered config delivers. After Grafana rolls out, fire a real test through its own notifier (a rendered-but-undeliverable pipeline is exactly the silent failure the alerts exist to prevent):

# Grafana's admin password lives in the grafana-initial-admin Secret.
# Test the provisioned contact point with its real, env-expanded recipients:
kubectl -n grafana exec deploy/grafana -- \
  wget -qO- --post-data='{"receivers":[{"name":"cluster-alerts-email",
    "grafana_managed_receiver_configs":[{"name":"cluster-alerts-email","type":"email",
    "settings":{"addresses":"<your-address>","singleEmail":false}}]}],
    "alert":{"annotations":{"summary":"alerting pipeline test"}}}' \
  --header='Content-Type: application/json' \
  "http://admin:$ADMIN_PW@localhost:3000/api/alertmanager/grafana/config/api/v1/receivers/test"

A status: "ok" and an email in the inbox means the pipeline works end to end.

docs.title: Grafana
docs.text:
New clusters will start with the grafana deployment blocked from starting a pod for lack of the grafana-initial-admin secret existing.

Creating this secret will enable grafana to start up and create an initial admin login. The secret should be left on the cluster after that as the deployment requires it, but making changes to it will not update any Grafana login unless Grafana’s persistent storage is reset.

docs.title: Creating grafana-admin-secret
docs.text:
Use this command to generate a usable secret with a random password:

kubectl -n grafana create secret generic grafana-initial-admin \
    --from-literal=admin-user=admin \
    --from-literal=admin-password="$(LC_ALL=C </dev/urandom tr -dc '[:alnum:]_' | head -c 32)"

docs.title: Sealed Secrets
docs.text:
The sealed-secrets controller will automatically generate a public+private keypair for each cluster that will be used to encrypt and decrypt secrets.

After any new cluster is provisioned, the generated keypair should be backed up externally (i.e. to a shared VaultWarden/BitWarden collection). With the keypair backed up, secrets can be decrypted locally or restored to a new cluster in the future.

docs.title: Back up generated keys
docs.text:
From the sealed-secrets README.md:

kubectl get secret \
    -n sealed-secrets \
    -l sealedsecrets.bitnami.com/sealed-secrets-key \
    -o yaml \
> cluster-sealed-secrets-master.key

Sensitive data!

Be sure to keep this file secure and delete from your working directory after uploading it to a secure credentials vault for backup.

Do not commit this file to source control

docs.title: Expose the public certificate
docs.text:
The controller serves its public certificate at /v1/cert.pem, which local kubeseal clients can fetch instead of pulling it from the cluster each time. Expose it through the Gateway API — see Exposing services for the full pattern and the ownership split.

Provide a Gateway and an HTTPRoute (leave the chart’s own ingress disabled):

gateway.yaml 
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: sealed-secrets
  namespace: sealed-secrets
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  gatewayClassName: eg
  listeners:
    - name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
      port: 443
      hostname: sealed-secrets.sandbox.k8s.phl.io
      tls:
        mode: Terminate
        certificateRefs:
          - name: sealed-secrets-gw-tls
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces:
          from: Same
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: sealed-secrets
  namespace: sealed-secrets
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: sealed-secrets
  rules:
    # Only the public cert is served — not the whole controller surface.
    - matches:
        - path: { type: Exact, value: /v1/cert.pem }
      backendRefs:
        - name: sealed-secrets
          port: 8080

Once deployed, local kubeseal clients can be configured to use it by setting the SEALED_SECRETS_CERT environment variable:

export SEALED_SECRETS_CERT=https://sealed-secrets.sandbox.k8s.phl.io/v1/cert.pem

docs.title: Deploying your project on the Civic Cloud
docs.text:
This is the path for a project team bringing an app onto a CodeForPhilly cluster, or adding something to an app that’s already here. It assumes you know your own app and Docker, and nothing about this repo.

There are two clusters, each with its own repo: sandbox (cfp-sandbox-cluster, *.sandbox.k8s.phl.io) and live (cfp-live-cluster, *.live.k8s.phl.io and real domains). They have the same layout. Everything lands on sandbox first.

Read in order the first time; each page is short.

  1. How deploys work: nothing is applied by hand. You change files, a pipeline turns them into manifests, and a second pull request shows you exactly what will change before it does.
  2. Your project in the repo: the handful of files that make up a project here, which ones you own, and the one rule about where raw manifests can go.
  3. Add a database: a PostgreSQL user and database on the shared cluster, in four files, none of them shared infrastructure.
  4. Connect your app: reading the connection settings and password, for helm and for kustomize apps, and the order to land things in.
  5. Data and backups: getting a psql shell, loading existing data, and what the backups do and don’t give you.
  6. Reference: the directory map and the gotchas, for when you already know the shape.

The running example is paws-data-pipeline, which is moving from a Postgres container inside its own pod to the shared cluster. Substitute your app’s name.

If you get stuck, ask in #civic-cloud on the Code for Philly Slack.

docs.title: Add a database
docs.text:
Both clusters run one PostgreSQL cluster for everyone, shared-cluster in the cloudnative-pg namespace, managed by CloudNativePG. You get a user and a database on it; you don’t run Postgres yourself.

What you get: PostgreSQL 18 with PostGIS and pgvector available, two instances with automatic failover, nightly backups plus continuous archiving stored off-Linode in Google Cloud Storage, and upgrades handled centrally.

Adding your database is four files in the cluster repo. None of them is in _infra/.

docs.title: 1. One password, sealed twice
docs.text:
Your Postgres user needs a password. cnpg reads it from a Secret in cloudnative-pg to set the role’s password; your app reads it from a Secret in your own namespace. Same password, two SealedSecrets.

Run this with KUBECONFIG pointing at the cluster you’re adding to (sandbox first); sealed values only decrypt on the cluster that sealed them.

APP=paws-data-pipeline; ROLE=paws
PW=$(openssl rand -base64 48 | tr -dc A-Za-z0-9 | head -c 40)
for ns in cloudnative-pg $APP; do
  kubectl create secret generic $ROLE-db-credentials -n $ns \
    --type kubernetes.io/basic-auth \
    --from-literal=username=$ROLE --from-literal=password="$PW" \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml \
  | kubeseal --controller-name sealed-secrets --controller-namespace sealed-secrets --format yaml \
  > $ns.secrets/$ROLE-db-credentials.yaml
done
unset PW

That writes cloudnative-pg.secrets/paws-db-credentials.yaml and paws-data-pipeline.secrets/paws-db-credentials.yaml. You never need to write the password down; once deployed, anyone with access to your namespace can read it back from the Secret.

docs.title: 2. The user: paws-data-pipeline.cnpg/role.yaml
docs.text:
A DatabaseRole is your Postgres user. cnpg creates it on shared-cluster and keeps it matching this spec, password included.

apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1
kind: DatabaseRole
metadata:
  name: paws
  namespace: cloudnative-pg        # required: cnpg wants this next to the Cluster
spec:
  cluster:
    name: shared-cluster
  name: paws
  login: true
  connectionLimit: 20              # the cluster allows 100 in total; be a good neighbour
  passwordSecret:
    name: paws-db-credentials
  databaseRoleReclaimPolicy: retain   # deleting this file does not drop the role

docs.title: 3. The database: paws-data-pipeline.cnpg/database.yaml
docs.text:
apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1
kind: Database
metadata:
  name: paws
  namespace: cloudnative-pg
spec:
  cluster:
    name: shared-cluster
  name: paws
  owner: paws
  extensions:                      # only if you need them
    - name: postgis
      ensure: present

Extensions go here, not in your migrations

Your role is not a superuser, so CREATE EXTENSION in a migration will fail. Declare the extension on the Database and the operator installs it before your app connects. Django, Rails, Prisma and the rest are happy once it exists.

docs.title: 4. Open the PR
docs.text:
Commit the four files, run the projection diff (how), and open the PR. You should see exactly four additions, all under cloudnative-pg/: a SealedSecret, a DatabaseRole, a Database, and a second SealedSecret under your namespace. Merge it and its deploy PR.

Then check it took:

kubectl -n cloudnative-pg get databaserole paws -o jsonpath='{.status}'
kubectl -n cloudnative-pg get database paws -o jsonpath='{.status.applied}{"\n"}'

You now have an empty database named paws, owned by a user named paws, reachable from inside the cluster at shared-cluster-rw.cloudnative-pg.svc.cluster.local. Nothing uses it yet.

Secret before role

If cnpg reconciles the DatabaseRole before its Secret exists, it marks the role failed and does not retry on its own. Landing both in one PR is enough. If it happens anyway: kubectl annotate cluster -n cloudnative-pg shared-cluster cnpg.io/reconciliationLoop="$(date +%s)" --overwrite, and check .status again.

Next: Connect your app.

docs.title: Connect your app
docs.text:
Your app needs five things: host, port, database, user, password. Four are plain configuration; the password comes from the Secret you sealed into your namespace.

host      shared-cluster-rw.cloudnative-pg.svc.cluster.local   (-ro for a read replica)
port      5432
database  paws
user      paws
password  Secret paws-db-credentials, key "password"

docs.title: Helm apps
docs.text:
Make the chart read these from values, with the password from a Secret. In templates/deployment.yaml:

env:
  - name: PGHOST
    value: {{ .Values.database.host }}
  - name: PGDATABASE
    value: {{ .Values.database.name }}
  - name: PGUSER
    value: {{ .Values.database.user }}
  - name: PGPASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: {{ .Values.database.passwordSecret }}
        key: password

If the chart currently runs its own Postgres container (PAWS did, as a sidecar in the app pod), remove it, or keep it behind a database.embedded: true default so local dev is unchanged. Cut a release and bump .holo/sources/<app>.toml to the new tag.

Then set the values in the cluster repo, paws-data-pipeline/release-values.yaml:

database:
  embedded: false
  host: shared-cluster-rw.cloudnative-pg.svc.cluster.local
  name: paws
  user: paws
  passwordSecret: paws-db-credentials

docs.title: Kustomize apps
docs.text: See balancer/ for a worked example: a balancer.env file rendered into a ConfigMap for the non-secret settings, the password merged into the app’s existing SealedSecret with kubeseal --merge-into, and the cnpg/ files included from the kustomization. One thing to know: a ConfigMap generated with a stable name does not restart your pod when it changes, so balancer carries a pod-template annotation it bumps on purpose.

docs.title: Order of operations
docs.text:
1. Database PR (previous page). Empty database exists.
  2. App change in your repo, tagged; pin bump here.
  3. Load your data if you have any.
  4. Values PR. The app rolls onto the shared cluster.

Steps 1 and 4 are small PRs in the cluster repo; step 2 is in yours. Doing it on sandbox first means step 4 on live is a copy.

Expect one restart if you change a sealed password

The deploy applies your SealedSecret and your Deployment within the same second, and the sealed-secrets controller takes about a second to write the Secret. A pod that starts in that gap reads the old value and restarts once. Harmless, and not a sign something is wrong.

Next: Data and backups.

docs.title: Getting a psql shell
docs.text:
Your team’s access covers your namespace, not cloudnative-pg, so the way in is a throwaway pod in your namespace with the credentials loaded:

kubectl -n paws-data-pipeline run psql --rm -it --restart=Never --image=postgres:18 \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"psql","image":"postgres:18","stdin":true,"tty":true,
    "command":["psql"],
    "env":[{"name":"PGHOST","value":"shared-cluster-rw.cloudnative-pg.svc.cluster.local"},
           {"name":"PGDATABASE","value":"paws"},
           {"name":"PGUSER","valueFrom":{"secretKeyRef":{"name":"paws-db-credentials","key":"username"}}},
           {"name":"PGPASSWORD","valueFrom":{"secretKeyRef":{"name":"paws-db-credentials","key":"password"}}}]}]}}'

The same pod with ["sleep","3600"] as the command is a workbench for pg_dump and pg_restore; kubectl cp files in and out.

docs.title: Loading existing data
docs.text:
Dump the old database in custom format, then restore as your own user, so you own everything you load:

# from wherever can reach the old database
pg_dump -Fc --no-owner --no-privileges -h OLDHOST -U OLDUSER -d OLDDB -f app.dump

# from the workbench pod, connected as paws
pg_restore -l app.dump | grep -vE " (EXTENSION|COMMENT - EXTENSION) " > list
pg_restore --no-owner --no-privileges -L list -d paws app.dump

The grep -v EXTENSION matters: the dump wants to CREATE EXTENSION, your user can’t, and the extension already exists from database.yaml. For a 50 MB database this takes seconds.

Then compare. Use exact counts, not pg_stat estimates (statistics aren’t carried by a restore):

select relname, (xpath('/row/c/text()', query_to_xml(
  format('select count(*) as c from %I.%I', schemaname, relname), false, true, '')))[1]::text::int
from pg_stat_user_tables order by 1;

Run it on both sides and diff the output.

docs.title: What the backups give you
docs.text:
• A nightly base backup at 04:00 UTC and continuous WAL archiving in between, so any point in the last 30 days is recoverable.
  • Stored in Google Cloud Storage, in a CodeForPhilly GCP project, deliberately not on Linode: they survive losing the Linode account.
  • Tested: both clusters have been restored into a scratch cluster and compared table by table.

docs.title: What they don’t give you
docs.text:
Backups are per cluster, not per database. Every database on shared-cluster shares one backup stream. Getting your database back to last Tuesday means recovering the whole cluster into a temporary cnpg Cluster (about two minutes) and dumping your database out of it. That’s an operator task: ask in #civic-cloud with the time you want, and keep in mind the other tenants’ data is in the same recovery.

If you want your own logical dumps too, the workbench pod above plus a CronJob in your namespace is all it takes, and pg_dump output is the portable form if your project ever leaves.

That’s the end of the path. Reference has the directory map and gotchas in one place.

docs.title: How deploys work
docs.text: The short version: you edit files on main, and a pipeline applies them to the cluster. Nobody runs kubectl apply by hand, and nothing is in the cluster that isn’t in the repo.

docs.title: Workspace, projection, deploy
docs.text:
The files on main are the workspace. They aren’t Kubernetes manifests yet; they’re the inputs: a pin to your app’s repo and tag, your helm values or kustomization, your sealed secrets.

A tool called hologit projects the workspace into plain manifests. It fetches your app’s chart or kustomization from the pinned tag, renders it with your values, and files every resource into a predictable path: <namespace>/<Kind>/<name>.yaml. That rendered tree is what gets applied.

you push to main
  → Build workflow projects the tree          → branch  releases/k8s-manifests
  → a "Deploy releases/k8s-manifests …" PR opens by itself, with a kubectl diff in its body
  → someone merges it                          → branch  deploys/k8s-manifests
  → Deploy workflow runs kubectl apply

Two things follow from this that are worth internalising on day one:

The deploy PR is your preview

Its body is kubectl diff against the real cluster: every line that will change. Read it even when your change is one value. Lenses and admission webhooks add things you didn’t type, and this is where you see them.

Deleting a file deletes the resource

The deploy’s last step removes anything that disappeared from the projected tree. Delete your app’s directory and the app is gone on the next deploy. This is a feature, but it means “clean up this old file” is a production change.

docs.title: Seeing the projection yourself
docs.text:
You don’t have to wait for the pipeline. From a clone with git holo installed:

git fetch origin
SHA=$(git holo project k8s-manifests-github 2>&1 | tail -1)
git diff --name-status origin/deploys/k8s-manifests "$SHA"   # which resources change
git show "$SHA":balancer/Deployment/balancer.yaml           # look at any one of them

Every PR to these repos includes that diff in its description. It’s the one review step that catches a values typo before it becomes a deploy.

docs.title: Sandbox first
docs.text:
Both clusters have the same layout on purpose. The habit is: land the change on sandbox, look at it running, then open the same change on live. Most live PRs are a sandbox PR with a hostname changed.

Next: Your project in the repo.

docs.title: Directory map
docs.text:
Path What it is Rule <app>/ The app’s workspace: release-values.yaml (helm) or kustomization.yaml (kustomize) Lens input. Only the chart values or kustomization belong here; other files are dropped by the render. <app>.secrets/ SealedSecrets for the app’s namespace Raw manifests. Seal against the cluster you’re deploying to. <app>.cnpg/ The app’s DatabaseRole + Database on shared-cluster Raw manifests; declare namespace: cloudnative-pg. A kustomize app may use <app>/cnpg/ instead. _infra/ cert-manager, Envoy Gateway, the cnpg operator and shared-cluster, backups Shared. Projects don’t edit it; in particular, no per-tenant managed.roles on the Cluster. _gateways/<app>.yaml Public hostname(s), TLS, and for helm apps the HTTPRoute One per app. _admins/<app>.yaml Namespace + deployment-admin ServiceAccount/Role Scoped to the app’s namespace. _docs/ This site Published on every push. .holo/sources/<name>.toml Upstream repo + ref Pin to a tag. .holo/branches/k8s-manifests/<app>/ Which upstream files land in <app>/ .holo/lenses/<app>.toml How <app>/ renders

The _ prefix means “not a workload namespace” and is dropped in the projected tree. The .suffix directories exist because <app>/ is spoken for by the lens.

docs.title: shared-cluster facts
docs.text: Service shared-cluster-rw.cloudnative-pg.svc.cluster.local:5432 (-ro for replicas) Version PostgreSQL 18, pinned by image digest in _infra/cloudnative-pg/shared-cluster.yaml; PostGIS 3.6 and pgvector 0.8 available Instances 2, automatic failover Connections max_connections 100; each role gets connectionLimit: 20 Backups Barman Cloud plugin → gs://cnpg-<cluster>; nightly 04:00 UTC + WAL; 30-day retention Operator CloudNativePG, chart in _infra/cloudnative-pg/operator

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Secret before role. A DatabaseRole reconciled before its passwordSecret exists is marked failed and not retried. Same PR is enough; otherwise nudge with kubectl annotate cluster -n cloudnative-pg shared-cluster cnpg.io/reconciliationLoop="$(date +%s)" --overwrite.
  • Pod before Secret. A changed SealedSecret and a Deployment in the same deploy can race by a second; the pod restarts once.
  • Not a superuser. Extensions go on the Database, not in migrations.
  • Statistics aren’t restored. n_live_tup reads 0 after a physical restore; compare with count(*).
  • DEBUG=false is true to Django when the app does bool(os.environ.get("DEBUG")); set it empty instead.
  • Deleting a file deletes the resource. Including your database objects (the role itself survives thanks to retain; the Database object’s data does too, but check before you clean up).

docs.title: Your project in the repo
docs.text:
A project is a small set of files in predictable places. Here they are for paws-data-pipeline; yours look the same with the name swapped.

.holo/sources/paws-data-pipeline.toml          ← where your code comes from, pinned to a tag
.holo/branches/k8s-manifests/paws-data-pipeline/helm-chart.toml
.holo/lenses/paws-data-pipeline.toml           ← how it's rendered (helm or kustomize)
paws-data-pipeline/release-values.yaml         ← your helm values (or kustomization.yaml)
paws-data-pipeline.secrets/*.yaml              ← SealedSecrets for your namespace
paws-data-pipeline.cnpg/*.yaml                 ← your database user + database (next page)
_gateways/paws-data-pipeline.yaml              ← your public hostname and TLS
_admins/paws-data-pipeline.yaml                ← namespace + a deployment-admin role for your team

docs.title: What you own
docs.text:
Everything with your app’s name in it is yours to change through a PR. The three .holo/ files rarely change after setup; release-values.yaml, .secrets/ and .cnpg/ are where day-to-day changes happen.

Directories starting with _ (_infra/, _gateways/, _admins/) are cluster-wide. You own your file inside _gateways/ and _admins/; _infra/ (cert-manager, Envoy Gateway, the Postgres operator) you should never need to touch.

docs.title: The one rule about <app>/
docs.text:
paws-data-pipeline/ is the input to a lens. For a helm app that means: the chart is fetched into it from your repo, release-values.yaml is applied, and the rendered output replaces the directory in the projected tree. Anything else you put in that directory is not rendered and silently disappears.

That’s why things that belong to your app but aren’t part of the chart live in sibling directories with a suffix: paws-data-pipeline.secrets/ and paws-data-pipeline.cnpg/. Those are raw manifests, applied as written, and routed to the right namespace by the namespace: they declare.

(A kustomize app can get away with a subdirectory instead, because kustomize passes raw resources through; balancer keeps its database files in balancer/cnpg/ and lists them in its kustomization. Either way is fine; the sibling directory works for both.)

docs.title: Pins
docs.text: .holo/sources/paws-data-pipeline.toml names a git ref in your repo. Make it a tag. Tracking refs/heads/master means a merge in your repo can change what’s deployed, or break the cluster build, with no PR here to review it. Cut a release, bump the pin, open the PR: that’s a deploy.

docs.title: Your namespace
docs.text:
Your app runs in a namespace with its name. _admins/<app>.yaml gives your team a deployment-admin ServiceAccount there, enough to see pods, read logs, exec and port-forward. It does not reach other namespaces, which matters for the database pages: your Postgres lives in cloudnative-pg, and you reach it from inside your own namespace.

Next: Add a database.

docs.text: Open https://echo-http.sandbox.k8s.phl.io/ to verify cluster connectivity and ingress.

docs.title: To 0.20.x
docs.text: cluster-template v0.20.x brings compatibility with Kubernetes 1.22

docs.title: Upgrade cert-manager APIs
docs.text:
Any manifests defining ClusterIssuer objects must be upgraded to the stable API:

diff --git a/cert-manager.issuers.yaml b/cert-manager.issuers.yaml
index ebd08997..8dba5834 100644
--- a/cert-manager.issuers.yaml
+++ b/cert-manager.issuers.yaml
@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
-apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1alpha2
+apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
 kind: ClusterIssuer

docs.title: Upgrade cert-manager CRDs
docs.text: If migrating from a pre-1.0 version of cert-manager to a post-1.0 version, you may need to manually delete all CRDs

docs.title: Upgrade sealed-secrets ingress config
docs.text:
The newer version of sealed-secrets has a new syntax for configuring its ingress:

diff --git a/sealed-secrets/release-values.yaml b/sealed-secrets/release-values.yaml
index eb3216c2..3fcef1d3 100644
--- a/sealed-secrets/release-values.yaml
+++ b/sealed-secrets/release-values.yaml
@@ -6,9 +6,5 @@ ingress:
   annotations:
     kubernetes.io/ingress.class: nginx
     cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
-  hosts:
-    - sealed-secrets.sandbox.k8s.example.com
-  tls:
-    - secretName: sealed-secrets-tls
-      hosts:
-        - sealed-secrets.sandbox.k8s.example.com
+  hostname: sealed-secrets.sandbox.k8s.example.com
+  tls: true

docs.title: Upgrade RBAC APIs for any service account manifests
docs.text:
diff --git a/admins/project-admin.yaml b/admins/project-admin.yaml
index dc5c52d0..b3fedfcc 100644
--- a/admins/project-admin.yaml
+++ b/admins/project-admin.yaml
@@ -14,7 +14,7 @@ metadata:
 ---

 kind: Role
-apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1beta1
+apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
 metadata:
   name: deployment-admin

docs.title: Check for deprecated APIs
docs.text:
After deploying v0.20.x, check for any locally-defined manifests using deprecated APIs before upgrading the host cluster to Kubernetes v1.22+.

Check for deployed objects with deprecated APIs:

kubent --target-version 1.22.0

Check for helm chart snapshots:

pluto detect-helm

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Before deploying an upgrade to v0.20.x, delete existing ingress-nginx jobs to prevent errors about immutable fields being changed:

kubectl -n ingress-nginx delete jobs ingress-nginx-admission-create ingress-nginx-admission-patch

For the same reason, also delete the prometheus-kube-state-metrics deployment:

kubectl -n prometheus delete deployment prometheus-kube-state-metrics

docs.title: To 1.0.x
docs.text: If upgrading from a version earlier than v0.20.x, follow the notes for upgrading to v0.20.x instead.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Before deploying an upgrade to v1.0.x, delete existing ingress-nginx jobs to prevent errors about immutable fields being changed:

kubectl -n ingress-nginx delete jobs ingress-nginx-admission-create ingress-nginx-admission-patch
